strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck in automated software engineering: localizing relevant code before patch generation.

SWELOC is potentially valuable: it draws from thousands of real repositories, pairs issues with actual modifications, excludes benchmark repositories, and applies hard-negative mining and consistency filtering.
The retrieve-and-rerank design is computationally attractive and achieves large improvements over strong pretrained retrievers on both SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench.

Evaluation spans file, module, and function granularity, includes ranking and agent-based baselines, and contains useful studies of filtering, training-set size, model initialization, and inference cost.
The paper is generally clear, and the appendix reports core optimization settings and substantial compute requirements.
weaknesses: The central method is technically incremental: SWERANK combines a conventional bi-encoder contrastive retriever with an existing listwise-reranking recipe. Most novelty lies in the automatically constructed dataset rather than the modeling.

Crucial reproducibility details are missing, including SWELOC's final size after filtering, collection time, repository list, deduplication criterion, code-parsing procedure, exact train split, candidate construction, and the mechanism for aggregating function scores into module and file rankings.

Reranker inference is underspecified. Training uses a window of ten candidates and supervises only the first identifier, yet results include Acc@15 and full ranked outputs. The paper does not explain sliding-window or permutation inference, decoding, candidate count, or how rankings beyond the first position are learned reliably.

The data labels are noisy proxies: every modified function is treated as relevant and every unmodified function as irrelevant, despite incidental edits, incomplete fixes, and relevant-but-unchanged functions. Filtering positives with the same pretrained retriever used for mining also preferentially retains easy lexical or semantic matches and may narrow dataset coverage.

The comparison is difficult to audit because agent results are imported from prior work while 26 SWE-Bench-Lite cases are excluded here. It is not made sufficiently explicit that all reported baseline numbers use exactly the same 274 examples, repository snapshots, localization definitions, and candidate extraction.

Some claims overstate the evidence. SWERANK does not uniformly beat GPT-4.1: it is lower on several SWE-Bench-Lite metrics and on some LocBench metrics. Cost analysis excludes indexing, embedding computation, hardware, latency, and memory, making the broad efficiency conclusion incomplete.
There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multi-seed results despite differences between leading systems sometimes being below one percentage point.
Scope is restricted to Python repositories, and the paper does not test cross-language transfer, temporal generalization, repository-level distribution shift, or downstream patch-generation gains.

The proposed dataset release lacks discussion of source-code licenses, redistribution permissions, personally identifying issue content, and security-sensitive material. The manuscript also provides no working artifact link, limiting current verifiability.

Several presentation errors reduce polish, such as Table 4 describing all evaluated rerankers as 7B despite including 3B and 32B models, duplicated or inconsistent references, and unclear terminology around modules versus classes.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in automated software engineering: accurately localizing code relevant to natural-language issues without the latency and expense of iterative agents.
SWELOC is potentially valuable: it draws supervision from real GitHub issues and patches at substantial scale and includes repository-level hard-negative mining.
The proposed system is computationally attractive and obtains strong reported results on both SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, including sizable improvements over its pretrained retriever backbones.

The evaluation covers file-, module-, and function-level localization, and includes useful analyses of filtering thresholds, training-set size, alternative model initializations, and estimated inference cost.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. SWERANK largely combines a standard contrastively trained bi-encoder with an existing listwise reranking paradigm; the main reranker modification is first-identifier supervision. The paper does not convincingly distinguish this contribution from straightforward task-specific fine-tuning.

SWELOC's labels are noisy proxies: every modified function is treated as relevant and every unmodified function as irrelevant, although patches often contain refactoring, bookkeeping, or incidental changes, while unmodified functions may still be semantically relevant. There is no manual label-quality audit.

The consistency filter is circular and may bias the dataset toward easy examples favored by CodeRankEmbed: an instance survives only when that existing model already ranks its positive highly. This can remove precisely the difficult cases that a new localization model should learn, and the paper does not analyze the resulting selection bias.

Essential dataset information is missing, including the final number of filtered issues and function-level instances, repository and temporal distributions, exact deduplication procedure, and train/validation splitting. The manuscript also contains a blank release link, so the central dataset, code, and models are not currently available for verification.

The reranker is under-analyzed. Training supervises only the first generated identifier, while inference requires a complete ranking, yet there are no comparisons against pointwise classification, pairwise ranking, full pseudo-rank supervision, or the pretrained reranker without SWELOC. Sensitivity to candidate-pool size and ordering is also absent.

The empirical evidence lacks uncertainty estimates, multiple training runs, or significance testing. Several headline improvements are only a few examples on the 274-instance SWE-Bench-Lite subset, making it unclear which differences are robust.

The comparison with agent systems is not fully controlled: agent numbers are imported from prior work, systems have different access patterns and candidate spaces, and the cost calculation omits retriever-side repository parsing, embedding, indexing, hardware, latency, and storage. Consequently, the broad superiority and cost-efficiency claims are stronger than the evidence supports.

Evaluation excludes 26 SWE-Bench-Lite cases without modified existing functions and assesses localization accuracy only, without showing whether better rankings improve downstream patch generation or issue resolution. The scope is also restricted to predominantly Python repositories.

The paper does not discuss licensing, privacy, sensitive content, or governance implications of redistributing code and issue text mined from thousands of public repositories. These concerns are material for the proposed dataset.

Presentation and reproducibility need refinement: important implementation and inference details are underspecified, some claims are overgeneralized (for example, improvement of 'any' embedding model), and there are several typographical, citation, and table-caption inconsistencies.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck in automated software engineering: accurately localizing issue-relevant code without the latency, cost, and brittleness of multi-step agents.

SWELOC is a potentially valuable task-specific resource, constructed from 3,387 repositories and 67,341 initial PR-codebase pairs with repository exclusion, source-overlap deduplication, consistency filtering, and hard-negative mining.

The evaluation is broad and convincing overall: it covers SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, three localization granularities, agentic systems, sparse retrieval, several dense retrievers, and multiple rerankers.

The reported improvements are substantial. For example, the large retriever reaches 82.12 function Acc@10 on SWE-Bench-Lite, while the large reranker reaches 88.69; on LocBench, the latter achieves 76.25 function Acc@15, exceeding the listed agent-based and ranking baselines.

The analysis usefully studies filtering thresholds, training-data scale, multiple retriever initializations, text- versus code-pretrained rerankers, model sizes, and inference cost. These results support the claim that SWELOC's value is not confined to one backbone.
The approach is technically straightforward but well motivated, clearly presented, and practically attractive; the small 137M retriever is especially compelling given its strong performance.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the main framework combines established bi-encoder retrieval, contrastive learning, hard-negative mining, and single-token listwise reranking. Much of the contribution therefore depends on the dataset and empirical execution.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although training hyperparameters are supplied, the promised code/data/model link is blank, and the paper does not clearly report the final number of training instances after consistency filtering, validation procedures, random seeds, or result variance.

The automatically derived labels are imperfect: every modified function is treated as relevant and every unmodified function as irrelevant. Refactorings or incidental edits can create false positives, while relevant but unchanged functions can become false negatives. Filtering with the same pretrained retriever used for mining may also bias SWELOC toward examples that embedding models already find easy.

No statistical uncertainty or significance testing is reported. This matters for relatively small evaluations such as the 274 retained SWE-Bench-Lite cases and for several close comparisons with GPT-4.1 and CodeRankLLM.

The efficiency analysis focuses on estimated per-instance API-equivalent cost and treats precomputed embeddings as negligible, but does not report end-to-end latency, indexing time, memory/storage requirements, hardware utilization, or amortization assumptions. Thus, the broad efficiency claim is only partially substantiated.

The scope is limited to Python repositories and localization accuracy. There is no downstream experiment showing that the improved rankings increase actual patch-generation or issue-resolution success, so claims about broader automated repair utility remain indirect.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations and ethics/data-governance discussion. For a dataset mined from public GitHub issues and code, licensing, attribution, personally identifying content, repository removal, and release governance should be addressed explicitly.
Training the largest models requires up to 16 GH200 GPUs, which limits accessibility and sits somewhat uneasily with the emphasis on efficiency, even though inference is relatively inexpensive.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in automated software engineering and presents a clear retrieve-and-rerank formulation that is substantially cheaper and faster than multi-step agentic localization.
SWELOC is a potentially valuable contribution: it contains real issue descriptions paired with code changes from thousands of repositories, with task-specific filtering and hard-negative mining.

The empirical results are strong across SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench. SWERANK consistently improves its base retrievers and rerankers and is competitive with or better than substantially more expensive agent-based systems.

The evaluation is unusually broad, including retriever and reranker comparisons, data-size and filtering ablations, model-capacity studies, multilingual transfer, retrieval-ceiling analysis, latency and token measurements, and a downstream repair experiment.
Results across multiple model families provide convincing evidence that much of the benefit comes from the task-specific training data rather than only a particular architecture.
weaknesses: The modeling contribution is technically modest: the bi-encoder, InfoNCE training, hard-negative mining, and LLM reranking components are largely standard. The dataset and empirical study, rather than a new learning method, constitute the principal novelty.

Dataset supervision equates every patch-modified function with a relevant location and every unmodified function with an irrelevant one. This can introduce incidental positives and false negatives, yet the paper provides no manual quality audit or estimate of label noise.

Consistency filtering retains examples that a pretrained retriever already ranks highly. This is potentially circular and may bias SWELOC toward lexically or semantically easy cases; the ablations demonstrate performance benefits but do not establish that the resulting dataset faithfully represents the full issue-localization distribution.

Data leakage controls are insufficiently documented. Although benchmark repositories are excluded and source-overlap deduplication is mentioned, the paper does not specify the deduplication algorithm, thresholds, collection dates, temporal cutoffs, or checks for issue-text and code contamination in pretrained base models.

Several central claims are overstated. SWERANK does not dominate GPT-4.1 across all reported localization metrics, and the statement that the reranker captures cross-function dependencies is not established by the complexity-stratified accuracy results alone.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript's code-and-model footnote lacks an actual URL, post-filtering dataset statistics are unclear, and important inference details such as reranking window application, prompts, output parsing, and handling of more candidates than fit in one window are not fully specified.
The results are reported without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This matters for the smaller SWE-Bench-Lite evaluation and for several relatively small reranker gains.

The cost and latency comparison is not fully controlled across hardware, hosted API pricing, model access, and system capabilities. Treating retrieval as negligible through precomputation also omits repository indexing costs, so the efficiency conclusions should be qualified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in automated software repair and motivates the efficiency advantages of retrieval-based localization clearly.
SWELOC is potentially valuable: it derives supervision from real issues and patches, mines repository-specific negatives, and explicitly excludes repositories from the evaluation benchmarks.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering SWE-Bench-Lite, LocBench, multilingual transfer, downstream repair, multiple model sizes, data scaling, filtering, negative mining, latency, and token usage.
The reported localization improvements are large and generally consistent across datasets and granularities. The small 137M retriever is especially promising from an efficiency perspective.

The manuscript is readable and well organized, with informative tables and figures. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/21bdd8daa108419a88dc1c29b6765a7e/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. The framework combines a conventional bi-encoder, InfoNCE training, hard-negative mining, and a single-token listwise reranker; consequently, much of the contribution rests on SWELOC and the reliability of its evaluation.

Critical inference details for the reranker are absent. Training uses ten candidates, yet reranking raises function Acc@10 from 82.12 to 88.69, which requires access to candidates outside the retriever's top ten. The paper never specifies the inference candidate depth, sliding-window procedure, aggregation method, or failure handling, making the central result difficult to interpret or reproduce.

SWELOC is insufficiently documented. The paper reports 67,341 initial PR-codebase pairs but not the final number of issues, function-level instances, repositories, or negatives after filtering; it also omits temporal coverage, split construction, deduplication details, and dataset-quality auditing. The advertised code link is blank, further weakening reproducibility.

The labels are only proxies for localization relevance: every modified function is treated independently as positive, while every unmodified function is treated as negative. Patches may contain refactoring or incidental edits, and relevant but unchanged functions may become false negatives. No manual validation estimates this noise or establishes that the filtering process preserves difficult cases.

Consistency filtering is circular and selection-biased: examples are retained only when an existing CodeRankEmbed model already places the positive in its top 20. This preferentially removes difficult or semantically indirect issues, but the paper does not characterize what is discarded or evaluate performance by retained-versus-filtered issue type.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Improvements on models from a small set of related families do not establish that SWELOC improves 'any embedding model'; a reranker trained with one positive at a time does not demonstrate that it captures cross-function dependencies; and results on Python-trained models across one multilingual benchmark do not establish broad language independence.

The efficiency analysis is not auditable. It does not explain how dollar costs for locally hosted models were calculated, excludes embedding/index construction, compares latency across apparently different hardware and API environments, and reports only 50 latency examples without variance. Table 5's stated 'up to 6X' cost-performance advantage also appears inconsistent with its own ratios, which are much larger.

The evaluation provides no confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or multi-seed variation despite only 274 SWE-Bench-Lite and roughly 560 LocBench examples. Modest downstream repair gains, such as 24.5 versus 22.6 Pass@1, therefore cannot be distinguished confidently from sampling or run variance.

Important reproducibility specifications remain unclear, including function/module extraction, handling of parsing failures and duplicate functions, prompt templates, candidate truncation/order at inference, embedding normalization and contrastive temperature, benchmark preprocessing, and exact baseline re-evaluation procedures.

There is no substantive discussion of licensing, privacy, removal requests, or redistribution constraints for mining and releasing code and issue text from thousands of GitHub repositories. Given that the dataset is presented as a central community resource, this omission is significant.

strengths: The manuscript presents a clear, practically important formulation of issue localization as task-specific code ranking, supported by a new training dataset and an efficient retrieve-and-rerank system. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/39423c860ea942b69aa3adce678214ed/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical results are strong and consistent across SWE-Bench-Lite, LocBench, and SWE-Bench Multilingual. SWERANK improves substantially over its initialization models and is competitive with or better than considerably more expensive agentic systems.

The evaluation is unusually broad: it includes multiple model scales and architectures, filtering and data-size analyses, iterative negative mining, capacity studies, retrieval-ceiling analysis, complexity and overlap breakdowns, latency and token measurements, qualitative examples, and downstream repair results.
The paper demonstrates that SWELOC benefits several independently initialized retrievers and rerankers, providing evidence that the dataset contribution is useful beyond the proposed model instances.

The method offers a compelling practical tradeoff: the small retriever is competitive despite having only 137M parameters, while the full framework achieves high localization accuracy with substantially lower inference cost and latency than agentic alternatives.

The paper is well organized, technically plausible, and supplies useful training details, including initialization, objectives, hyperparameters, context limits, negative sampling, and computational resources.
weaknesses: The core modeling techniques—bi-encoder contrastive learning, hard-negative mining, and LLM reranking—are largely established. The main novelty lies in task-specific data construction and empirical execution rather than a fundamentally new learning method.

The automatically derived supervision treats every function changed by a pull request as relevant and every unchanged function as irrelevant. Incidental refactors, auxiliary changes, and incomplete patches can therefore introduce label noise; the paper does not include a human audit quantifying this noise.

Consistency filtering retains examples whose positives already rank within the top 20 under CodeRankEmbed. This may bias SWELOC toward cases recognizable by an existing retriever and underrepresent genuinely difficult issue-to-code relationships.

Essential dataset accounting is incomplete: the paper reports 67,341 initial PR/codebase pairs but does not clearly state the final number of filtered PRs, training instances, positives, or negatives. The code-and-model footnote also lacks a visible URL, limiting immediate reproducibility assessment.

Results are reported as point estimates without confidence intervals, statistical tests, or variation across training seeds. This matters for several close comparisons, such as SWERANKLLM versus GPT-4.1 and differences among reranker variants.

The cost analysis omits some methodological details, including pricing assumptions, indexing and embedding costs, hardware amortization, and whether all systems were measured under comparable deployment conditions. Accordingly, the precise cost-efficiency ratios should be interpreted cautiously.

The strongest results require a 7B retriever and 32B reranker trained using substantial GH200 compute. Although inference is efficient relative to agents, this training footprint weakens the broader efficiency narrative and is not discussed in environmental or accessibility terms.
